title: Effort and Ease
speaker: Jonathan Prescott
summary: Jonathan Prescott takes up Right Diligence, or Right Effort, as a dynamic balance between effort and ease. Jonathan tells of sitting alone on a curb at age three, of two years spent on an introductory koan, and of Anne Aitken's thirteen years on hers. Zen is strong on effort, which can solidify the ego, while Jonathan's own Plum Village tradition can turn into summer camp and settle for ease. Jonathan works the balance through sitting posture, through breathing, where little John makes the effort to breathe in and Buddha nature breathes out, and through concentration, beginning with an entering-the-hall gatha and closing with Ajahn Chah's line about letting go a little, a lot, or completely.

Just to recap for the recording, what I'd like to talk about is Right Diligence, or Right Effort.
I think it's a really important aspect of our practice.
I've noticed that some traditions lean towards diligence more than others, and we have a lot to learn from each other in this.
So that's what I'd like to do: touch on diligence.
Let's start with long-term diligence.
For some reason, all of us here have entered the stream of practice.
How wonderful that is, that we found our way here, and how rare.
For me, I seem to have somehow been born to this.
My parents love to tell the story, especially as they're 90 years old now.
I hear this story a lot, over and over again.
I used to sit on the curb as a three-year-old by myself, and just sit.
My parents were so baffled by this, because my parents are quite extroverted people, and I'm a very quiet contemplative, and apparently I was wired for this from the very beginning.
I don't remember doing that, but that's what they tell me.
I've been at a formal contemplative practice for over 40 years now.
So somehow I jumped into this stream, and I just didn't climb back out again.
No benefit, no praise to me over that.
I just did it.
I felt like it was the most important thing.
Typically we tend to dip our toes in and out of practice, particularly at the earlier stages, and I know I did this.
I dipped my toes in.
I'd say, "Oh, I like that, but oh, I don't like that," and take my toe back out.
I did that over and over again.
I look back on that and think, gosh, what a shame.
I bypassed so much benefit I could have had.
Early on I could have spent much more time personally with Thich Nhat Hanh than I did, because I was dipping my toe in and out.
So I regret that a little bit.
I'll return to long-term diligence a little bit later, but for now let's just agree that long-term diligence means staying in the stream of practice.
Whether we do that by intention or stubbornness or just chance, the old-timers among us are the ones who just didn't climb back out of the river.
They got in and just didn't climb out.
After all, "Roshi" means old teacher: somebody who stayed in the river long enough to really get good and wet.
That's long-term diligence.
How about short-term diligence?
Really the question here is how we express diligence in our daily practice.
I like to think of diligence, or right effort, as the balance between effort and ease.
Balance between effort and ease.
Let's start with effort.
Zen people really know how to make effort, right?
Especially Japanese Zen people.
Yeah.
We know how to sit still for hours.
We know how to follow the form really precisely.
We know how to wrestle with koans, sometimes for years.
I spent two years on my introductory koan.
Two years I wrestled with that.
That was diligent on my part, going down all these different roads, all these roads.
My teacher would say, [unclear: "well, now to go"].
But I think I've got a lot of diligence, and then I think about Anne Aiken, Robert Aitken's wife, who spent 13 years on the same introductory koan.
She's all over me in terms of diligence.
She was really diligent with that.
So we know how to do effort.
But effort alone isn't enough, because diligent effort can also be an expression of our ego.
You might notice this in yourself: look how still I can sit.
Or look how I can sit through pain.
Look at me.
Look how precisely I can follow the form.
Much better than you.
So this diligent effort can also be a way of solidifying our ego.
Many of us first enter the zendo with this dream of becoming enlightened, of attaining something.
But these are just the ego's dreams, and too much effort can just solidify that.
So we have to be careful about effort.
Effort alone isn't enough.
That brings us to ease.
Thich Nhat Hanh taught that if your practice doesn't include happiness, you're not practicing well.
He famously said, happiness is here and now.
In the Thich Nhat Hanh tradition, we love to make songs out of these little poems that Thay wrote.
So this one is:
*Happiness is here and now.
I have dropped my worries.
Nowhere to go.
Nothing to do.
No longer in a hurry.
Happiness is here and now.*
He didn't say grim determination is here and now.
He said happiness is here and now.
This makes sense, because when we are free, the present moment is a wonderful moment.
It's a happy moment, even when it's filled with things we don't like.
This is one of the markers of freedom: that we are free of the negative emotions, free of grimness, and happiness arises.
So my tradition's really good at ease.
But that's a trap too.
Many people come to Plum Village as though it were a summer camp.
And frankly, it kind of is.
It really kind of is.
People see a new way and they leave with an idea of freedom, but without much actual freedom, without the diligence to make that freedom a reality in their own lives.
So in my tradition we can get lost in the ease part of it, just like other traditions might be stereotypically getting trapped in the effort.
My tradition gets trapped in the ease.
So effort and ease should be in balance.
Too much effort just solidifies our striving, and too much ease leaves us the victim of our habit energies.
So we end up sitting on the knife's edge.
Balance, effort, and ease.
What does it look like to sit on the knife's edge in real life?
How about sitting posture?
The effort for a sitting posture would be holding our body with stillness and balance and dignity.
But ease would be holding stillness, balance, and dignity with the least effort necessary.
We can relax even the muscles that hold our posture.
We don't clamp down, but we don't fall down.
We find the middle way, balancing ease and effort.
You might enjoy looking at your body right now and noticing, as you sit in your upright posture that has dignity and balance, whether there's any tension that you can actually relax.
It's not necessary for holding you in that dignity.
It is possible to hold ourselves in that kind of still posture with very little effort, and I find that enjoyable.
If I'm making too much effort, I can't sustain it.
My muscles get tired, my mind gets tired.
So that's balancing effort and ease in my sitting posture.
How about in our breathing?
That's another way we can balance our effort and our ease.
The effort is in drawing in the breath.
To draw in a breath takes bodily effort.
Your diaphragm has to drop down and create a vacuum in your lungs that pulls in the air from outside.
This takes effort, and it's a fundamental bodily effort.

I've been present with a lot of people when they died, and I've noticed that some of those people, after they've actually lost the strength to draw in more air to their body, continue to make subtle bodily efforts to bring in air.
So you might see something like no more strength left to pull in the air.
But there's something so fundamental about breathing that it's one of the last bodily movements to cease.
It takes effort, because dying people lose the strength to make that effort.
But breathing also contains ease.
When we breathe out, we just simply release and the breath comes out by itself.
No effort to breathe out at all.
This is the way I like to breathe.
I make an effort to breathe in whatever arises.
Whether I like it or not, I breathe it in.
Right now, it's like this.
But breathing out, little John doesn't breathe out.
I let Buddha nature breathe out.
No effort at all.
What I've just breathed in, Buddha nature breathes out the response.
John makes the effort to breathe in.
That's the agreement.
I've got this body.
I'll use it.
I'll accept it.
Just like this.
But Buddha nature is what breathes out, and that takes no effort at all whatsoever.
You might enjoy breathing in this way too.

You might notice just now, in the next breath, the effort of breathing in, the effort of accepting life as it is in this moment, and then breathing out, completely letting go, trusting that deep well of love and compassion to be what breathes out.
One more real-life example of this balance would be in concentration.
Buddhism uses all kinds of different concentration practices, from just sitting, to Mu, to jhanas, to all different sorts of concentration practices.
But concentration also can be thought of as sitting on the knife edge between effort and ease.
The effort part, for me, involves setting an intention.
When I want to come and sit in the morning, when I enter the zendo, I set an intention.
I recite a gatha as I come in the door.
*Entering the meditation hall, I see my true self.
As I sit down, I vow to transform all disturbances.*
That's setting my intention as I walk in the door.
Oftentimes I walk in the door with a kind of momentum that is from whatever I've been doing previously.
Without setting an intention, that momentum will be what sits on the cushion.
So if I want to be concentrated, I need to interrupt that momentum and replace it with a momentum that I know is healthy, not just one that I inherited from the last moment.
So I say my gatha, and then I sit down on my cushion, and I slow, and I begin to make that effort to notice whatever disturbances are arising and to transform them.
Very often I'll need to start with a practice to concentrate my mind.
That might be counting my breath, or that might be diligently cutting off the mind road, in Aitken Roshi's phrase.
I do this over and over and over again, begin again and again and again, until I don't need to anymore.
That's when ease comes in.
As my momentum settles, I can throttle back on that effort, all that concentrated effort that I brought to it.
I can throttle that back, and I can lean into the ease as it naturally arises.
For me, ease is the natural state of my calm awareness.
My ego doesn't want to be at ease.
But as my ego lets go, I start to see the calm and ease where the very water I had been disturbing with my ego's activities.
I've been disturbing the water, rippling it, rippling it, rippling it.
When I use those concentration practices, the water slowly stills, and all my striving and effort calms with the water.
That's ease, to sit there.
I like the way Ajahn Chah put this.
He said, "If you want a little freedom, let go a little.
If you want a lot of freedom, let go a lot.
If you want complete freedom, let go completely."
And what are we letting go of?
In this case, it's our own effort.
So concentration requires this dynamic balance between effort and ease.
Too much ease at first means I'm just swept away by the currents of my mind.
But too much effort later means that I'm obscuring the very Buddha nature inherent in the spaciousness that is arising.
Balance, effort, and ease.
Okay, so diligence is a dynamic thing.
You might be picking up on that.
It's not a fixed point that we grab on to.
There's no single correct balance to find, and once you find it: "I've got that."
Yeah.
There's nothing we can obtain and hold on to here.

It's about placing one foot in effort and one foot in ease and living in that dynamic balance, just like we put half our weight on the left foot, half our weight on the right foot, and live in that dynamic balance.
Earlier I broke right effort into short-term and long-term, and I want to undo that, because really they're exactly the same thing.
In both cases, whether it's long-term diligence or short-term diligence, we begin with effort, and then we end up relaxing into ease.
Habits are really hard to break, as you know, and we come to practice with a lot of habits.
So we start practice with a lot of effort, and sometimes it's really, really hard.
We don't understand what's going on, but we just keep coming back to the form: effort, effort, effort, effort.
But if we're still expending that kind of effort after 10 or 20 years, we're probably stuck, right?
Because we've confused the effort for the liberation.
They're not the same thing, but they're related.
After a lot of effort, then we relax into this ease, and we see that life is fine just as it is, that I'm fine just as I am.
But boy, does it take a lot of diligent effort to get there, to see that.
It's really interesting, isn't it?

If you remember anything about my visit today, I would hope that it's this: that right diligence is a dynamic balance between effort and ease, and that we make an effort to breathe in life as it is in the here and now, and we respond with the ease of our true self.
Well, thank you so much for your kind attention.
Now, Des, is it my understanding that we have time for discussion?
**Participant:** Yes, we do.
We have plenty of time, so we'll open it up to everyone.
